title: API 653 Training in Billings, MT: Tank Inspector Exam Prep
description: API 653 exam prep for Billings tank inspectors: self-paced online with instructor Q&A, covering refinery, pipeline and terminal tanks, SPCC and hot taps.
h1: API 653 Training in Billings, Montana: Online Exam Prep for Refinery, Pipeline and Terminal Tank Inspectors
html:
API 653 exam prep for tank inspectors in the Billings area

Billings is a storage town as much as a refining town. Crude arrives from Canada and the Rockies and waits in tanks before it is run; finished fuel leaves by pipeline for terminals across Montana, North Dakota and eastern Washington; and the refineries keep their own fields of crude, intermediate, product and asphalt tanks. Field-erected steel tanks of that kind are inspected to API 653, and their formal inspections call for an inspector who holds the API 653 Aboveground Storage Tank Inspector certification.

Atlantis NDT's API 653 course is online and self-paced, with an instructor who answers your questions, and you can begin when you enrol. There is no Atlantis classroom in Billings. The American Petroleum Institute sets the eligibility rules in Annex D of API 653, administers the examination in person at Prometric test centres and issues the certification to those who pass.

Tankage around Billings, in the operators' own figures

The table lists what the operators themselves have published. It is not a complete inventory: the Phillips 66 and CHS tank farms are not broken down in these sources.

Operator and locationWhat is published
Par Pacific, Billings refinery and logistics2.848 million barrels of tankage at Billings and 4.1 million barrels in all across the refinery and logistics sites, as described when Par completed its purchase from ExxonMobil in 2023
Par Pacific, product terminalsBozeman and Helena, wholly owned, 89,000 barrels each; Missoula, 50% interest, 368,000 barrels; Thompson Falls, 50%, 140,000 barrels; Spokane, wholly owned, 350,000 barrels; Moses Lake, 171,000 barrels across six tanks with varying interests
CHS, Front Range PipelineCrude storage at Laurel, Santa Rita and Cut Bank on a line carrying more than 65,000 barrels a day from the Canadian border to the Laurel and Billings refineries
CHS, Cenex PipelineRefined products from the Laurel and Billings refineries to terminals at Glendive, Minot and Fargo
Enbridge, Express pipelineStorage tank terminals at Hardisty in Alberta and at Buffalo and Edgar in Montana, about 3 million barrels together, according to the Canada Energy Regulator

A Billings candidate may inspect a large refinery crude tank one month and a small mountain-town products terminal the next. The API 653 rules are the same; the service, floor design and regulator change.

Which rule sends an API 653 inspector to a Montana tank

Three federal regimes do most of the work here, and they ask for API 653 in different ways.

  • Oil spill prevention (SPCC). Under 40 CFR 112.8(c)(6), a facility must test or inspect each aboveground container on a regular schedule and whenever it makes material repairs, following industry standards. EPA's fact sheet names API 653 as the standard typically used for field-erected tanks and STI SP001 for welded shop-fabricated and small field-erected tanks. It also says trained facility staff can usually make the frequent visual checks, while formal API 653 inspections need an API 653 certified inspector.
  • Pipeline breakout tanks. 49 CFR 195.432 has three parts. Breakout tanks not covered by the other two are inspected at least once each calendar year, at intervals of no more than 15 months. Atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks are inspected for physical integrity to API 653, except that its risk-based internal inspection procedures in section 6.4.3 cannot set the internal interval. Tanks built to API 2510 are inspected under section 6 of API 510.
  • Process safety. Refinery tanks in a covered process fall under the mechanical integrity element of federal OSHA's process safety management standard, which applies directly because Montana has no OSHA State Plan, and under EPA's Risk Management Program, whose section 68.73 lists storage tanks among the equipment it covers.

The regime decides who sets the schedule and what records an auditor asks for; the exam tests API 653's own rules.

Hot asphalt, insulated shells and the examined damage mechanisms

Two of the three refineries make asphalt in volume: EIA rates CHS at Laurel and Par Montana at 19,800 and 14,500 barrels per stream day of asphalt and road oil, and asphalt is kept hot in insulated, heated tanks. That puts corrosion under insulation on tank shells and roofs near the top of a Billings tank inspector's list. RP 575 covers the inspection of insulated tanks, and API 653 itself says insulation needs removing only to the extent necessary to judge the condition of the shell or roof.

CUI is one of the ten RP 571 mechanisms in the current API 653 Body of Knowledge. The others are atmospheric corrosion, brittle fracture, caustic corrosion, caustic stress corrosion cracking, concentration cell corrosion, ethanol stress corrosion cracking, microbiologically influenced corrosion, soil corrosion and sulfuric acid corrosion. Several have Billings relevance worth noting while you study:

  • Brittle fracture matters wherever tanks see cold metal temperatures, which in Montana means most of the winter.
  • Ethanol stress corrosion cracking is a concern wherever fuel ethanol is received and stored for blending into gasoline, typically at product terminals.
  • Sulfuric acid corrosion applies to acid storage. EIA lists alkylation capacity at all three refineries, but which alkylation acid each uses is a site detail to confirm, not something to assume.
  • Soil corrosion and MIC attack floors from below, which leads to the next section.

Floors on Yellowstone terrace ground

The Billings refineries sit beside the Yellowstone River, and Montana DEQ's fact sheet for the Phillips 66 site describes what lies under it: clay-silts from the surface to about 6 feet, sandy gravels from about 6 to 22 feet, and Colorado Shale bedrock at roughly 22 feet, on an alluvial terrace of the river. Layered ground of that kind can drain freely in one layer and hold water in another, and a tank floor's underside, its foundation and its cathodic protection all have to be judged against it.

For the exam, this is three blocks of study. Settlement evaluation in API 653 Annex B covers edge settlement, bottom settlement near the shell and localised settlement remote from the shell, and the Body of Knowledge also asks you to work out the number of settlement survey points. Floor evaluation in section 4 and the internal inspection intervals in section 6 rest on soil-side and product-side corrosion rates and on the safeguards, such as release prevention barriers, cathodic protection and linings, that API 653 credits. And RP 651 on cathodic protection and RP 652 on bottom linings explain what those safeguards do and how they fail. Know where each topic sits in the documents, because a single floor question can draw on more than one of them.

Cold plate, toughness and hot taps

Cold weather enters the exam through toughness. The Body of Knowledge asks you to determine a tank's design metal temperature, the material group of a plate from API 650, whether impact testing is required and whether impact test values are acceptable. In service, the same question decides whether a tank can be hot tapped.

API 653 allows a nozzle to be welded onto a tank in service under its hot tapping rules, and the Body of Knowledge asks you to calculate the minimum spacing between a new hot tap and an existing nozzle. In the third edition of API 653 (December 2001, with the 2003 addendum), the edition published at law.resource.org, the hot tapping rules are in section 9.14; the current Body of Knowledge points to 9.15, so check the numbering in your edition. That older text sets tighter limits for shell plate of unknown toughness thicker than 1/2 in. with a minimum shell design metal temperature below its exemption curve: nozzles no larger than NPS 4, plate at or above that temperature for the whole hot tapping operation, and every nozzle reinforced.

Worked example: a new connection on a Billings crude tank

A pipeline operator wants a new 4 in. connection on a 120 ft diameter crude tank without taking it out of service. The bottom course is A36 plate, thickness measured at 0.580 in. around the proposed location, and the maximum liquid level is 40 ft above the bottom of that course. The highest specific gravity of the stored crude is 0.93. Work it with the formulas from the third edition text, then confirm each against your own edition.

  1. Toughness. The plate is thicker than 1/2 in. If its toughness is unknown and the tank's minimum shell design metal temperature falls below the exemption curve, the NPS 4 limit, the temperature condition and full reinforcement all apply. A 4 in. nozzle is within the size limit; anything larger would not be.
  2. Spacing. The minimum toe-to-toe spacing to the nearest existing nozzle is the square root of RT, with R the shell radius in inches and T the plate thickness in inches: R = 60 ft × 12 = 720 in., so √(720 × 0.580) = √417.6 = 20.4 in.
  3. Thickness. The same text requires shell thickness readings at a minimum of four places around the circumference of the proposed nozzle location before work starts.
  4. Shell minimum. For the whole course, tmin = 2.6(H − 1)DG ÷ SE. The text's Table 4-1 gives S = 24,900 lbf/in.² for A36 in the lower two courses (the smaller of 0.80Y and 0.429T, rounded), and E = 1.0 for a butt-welded tank built to API 650 seventh edition or later. With H − 1 = 39, tmin = 2.6 × 39 × 120 × 0.93 ÷ 24,900 = 11,316 ÷ 24,900 = 0.454 in.
  5. Intervals. The remaining corrosion allowance is 0.580 − 0.454 = 0.126 in., or 126 mils. With a shell corrosion rate of 4 mils a year, the external ultrasonic thickness interval is the smaller of RCA/2N = 126 ÷ 8 = 15.8 years and 15 years, so 15 years. The external inspection by an authorised inspector is the lesser of 5 years and RCA/4N = 7.9 years, so 5 years.

Often a cap, not the calculation, decides the answer. That happens a lot in interval work, which is why the caps deserve the same attention as the formulas.

Routes into API 653 for Billings tank people

Annex D of API 653 sets the eligibility rules: a bachelor's degree in engineering or technology with one year supervising or performing tank inspection; a two-year degree or certificate with two years in design, construction, repair, operation or inspection of tanks, one of them in inspection; a high school diploma with three years; or five or more years with no formal education. The experience must come from the last 10 years and API verifies it. The API 653 certification requirements page goes into the detail.

Tank work around Billings produces candidates by several routes. Gaugers and terminal operators know tanks in service, and City College at Montana State University Billings lists gaugers among the careers its process plant technology degree leads to; they usually need a move into inspection to complete the inspection year. Welders and boilermakers who build and repair tanks have the construction years and know Section IX. NDT technicians who scan floors, take shell thickness readings and test welds are already performing inspection work, and the NDT training in Billings page covers the method certifications behind it. Pipeline technicians who look after breakout tanks are close to the code, because 49 CFR 195.432 names API 653 for their tanks. The API 653 tank inspection guide explains what each inspection includes.

Studying API 653 around the Montana tank season

Out-of-service inspections need a tank emptied, cleaned and opened. If your site, like many in cold climates, plans that work for the milder months, a self-paced course lets you load the study into the rest of the year. Spend the quieter months on the material that needs memory: the inspection interval rules and the tables the Body of Knowledge marks for closed-book use, which include Table 6.1, used in setting internal inspection intervals, the joint efficiency Tables 4.2a and 4.2b, and Tables 10.1a, 10.1b and 10.2a in the disassembly and reconstruction section. Spend the weeks before the exam on timed open-book work in API 650 and API 653: material groups, impact testing figures, Annex B settlement and the hot tap and nozzle tables. Whenever a figure or table reads two ways, send it to the instructor rather than guessing.

Sponsoring tank inspectors from a Billings refinery, pipeline or terminal

Refineries, pipeline operators, terminal companies and tank contractors can enrol several candidates at once, and fees are quoted on request. Each candidate applies to API separately, so a sponsor's most useful work is keeping clear records of each person's tank inspection experience and timing study so that it does not collide with the outage season. Plan for recertification too: every three years an API 653 holder needs at least 20% of their time in the period spent performing or supervising tank inspection, 24 continuing professional development hours across at least two categories and, every six years, a web-based quiz on code changes.

faq.q: Is there an API 653 course I can attend in person in Billings?
faq.a: Not from Atlantis. There is no Atlantis classroom in the Billings area; the API 653 course is online and self-paced, with an instructor answering questions, and you can begin when you enrol. The examination is taken in person at a Prometric test centre once API has approved your application, so check the locator early and plan the trip if the nearest centre with a seat is some distance away.

faq.q: Our pipeline's Montana tanks are breakout tanks. Does API 653 apply to them?
faq.a: For atmospheric and low-pressure steel breakout tanks, yes: 49 CFR 195.432(b) requires their physical integrity to be inspected to API 653. Breakout tanks built to API 2510 are inspected under section 6 of API 510 instead, and any other breakout tanks under the annual inspection in paragraph (a). The rule also excludes API 653's risk-based internal inspection procedures in section 6.4.3, so internal intervals must be set by the code's other methods.

faq.q: Do the small shop-built tanks at a bulk plant need an API 653 inspector?
faq.a: Usually not under API 653 itself. EPA's SPCC guidance describes API 653 as the standard typically used for field-erected tanks and STI SP001 as the one for welded shop-fabricated and small field-erected tanks, with its own inspector qualifications. The facility's SPCC plan, which a Professional Engineer helps set and must certify if it departs from an industry standard, records which standard applies to each container.

faq.q: What if the shell corrosion rate of a tank is not known?
faq.a: API 653 sets a default. In the third edition text, when the rate is not known the maximum interval between external ultrasonic thickness measurements is five years, and rates can be estimated from tanks in similar service measured within that period. Once a rate is known, the interval becomes the smaller of RCA/2N and 15 years. Check the same clauses in your edition; the structure is the part exam questions rely on.

faq.q: Will I have to answer questions on API 653 tables without the book?
faq.a: Possibly. The Body of Knowledge marks some tables with an asterisk and says candidates may be expected to answer questions on them without access to the documents. They include Table 6.1, used for internal inspection intervals, the joint efficiency Tables 4.2a and 4.2b, and Tables 10.1a, 10.1b and 10.2a on disassembly and reconstruction. Learn those well enough to use from memory and leave the rest for the open-book half.

faq.q: I am a gauger at a terminal near Billings. Can I qualify for API 653?
faq.a: Gauging experience can count toward the operation side of the longer eligibility routes, but every route needs at least a year spent supervising or performing tank inspection, and API decides what it accepts. Many gaugers get there by assisting inspectors during out-of-service inspections and moving into an inspection role. Document the work carefully, because API verifies it.

faq.q: Can a terminal company enrol several tank inspectors together?
faq.a: Yes. A terminal or pipeline company can enrol a group, with fees quoted on request. Each person studies at their own pace and puts questions to the instructor individually, which works for staff spread across terminals in different towns. Every candidate still applies to API in their own name and books their own Prometric appointment after approval.
